extracted_claims.text: AI systems used for recruitment and selection of persons, including CV-sorting/filtering tools that materially influence candidate outcomes, are classified as high-risk under Annex III of the EU AI Act.

High-risk AI systems must comply with requirements including risk management systems (Art. 9), data governance (Art. 10), technical documentation (Art. 11), record-keeping (Art. 12), transparency/instructions for deployers (Art. 13), human oversight (Art. 14), and accuracy (Art. 15).
Providers of high-risk AI systems have obligations under Article 16, including quality management systems (Art. 17), documentation keeping (Art. 18), and automatically generated logs (Art. 19).
Deployers of high-risk AI systems have obligations under Article 26, including corrective actions and duty of information (Art. 20) and cooperation with competent authorities (Art. 21).
Article 27 of the AI Act obliges certain deployers of high-risk AI systems to conduct a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (FRIA) before initial deployment.
Article 4 requires organizations to ensure AI literacy among staff involved in the operation and use of AI systems.
Article 50 requires transparency notices to candidates for certain AI systems, with an effective date described as August 2026.
Article 50(2) marking/detection obligations have a compliance deadline of 2 December 2026 for providers of AI systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026.
The EU's Digital Omnibus on AI has deferred formal enforcement of Annex III high-risk system obligations (including hiring tools) to 2 December 2027, moved from the original 2 August 2026 date.

The AI Act Service Desk timeline states that obligations regarding Annex III high-risk systems enter into force on 2 December 2027, and obligations for high-risk systems embedded in regulated products (Annex I) enter into force on 2 August 2028.

Several news/blog sources state that operational enforcement for high-risk AI obligations (including hiring) begins on 2 August 2026, with national market surveillance authorities gaining full investigatory and sanctioning powers from that date.
Penalties for non-compliance with high-risk AI obligations can reach up to €15 million or 3% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher (except for SMEs/startups, where it is whichever is lower).
Penalties for prohibited AI practices (e.g., emotion recognition in workplaces) can reach up to €35 million or 7% of global annual turnover.
Supplying incorrect, incomplete, or misleading information to authorities can draw fines up to €7.5 million or 1% of worldwide annual turnover.
The Digital Omnibus on AI extended the 'whichever is lower' fine calculation rule in part to small mid-cap companies in July 2026.

National market surveillance authorities, not the European Commission directly, will undertake most compliance investigations and enforcement actions under the AI Act, exercising powers under Regulation 2019/1020.
Penalties for AI Act violations could be applied starting August 2, 2025, except for General-Purpose AI Model obligations, which take effect August 2, 2026.

Germany's Federal Cabinet adopted a draft AI Market Surveillance and Innovation Promotion Act on 10 February 2026, designating the Bundesnetzagentur as market surveillance authority, but the law has not yet passed the Bundestag/Bundesrat.
No specific enforcement actions or fines against any company for AI hiring tool non-compliance are documented in the available sources.
GDPR Article 22, limiting fully automated decision-making including rejections, continues to apply alongside AI Act obligations for hiring tools.
An AI system in Annex III may be exempt from high-risk classification if it performs a narrow procedural task or does not materially influence decision-making outcomes, per Article 6(3) derogation.

report:
# Compliance Requirements for High-Risk AI Hiring Tools Under the EU AI Act

## Executive Summary
AI hiring tools—including CV-screening systems that materially affect candidate outcomes—are classified as high-risk under Annex III of the EU AI Act, triggering obligations spanning risk management, data governance, human oversight, transparency, and fundamental rights impact assessments ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/employment-0)). However, enforcement timing is contested: the EU's Digital Omnibus on AI has reportedly deferred formal Annex III enforcement from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027 (high confidence), though many commercial and legal-analysis sources still cite August 2026 as operative. No documented enforcement actions or fines against any company for AI hiring tool non-compliance currently exist (high confidence).

## Key Findings

### Classification as High-Risk
AI systems used for recruitment and selection—including CV-sorting/filtering tools that materially influence candidate outcomes—are classified as high-risk under Annex III (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/employment-0), [Recital 57](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/recital-57)). An exemption exists under Article 6(3) where a system performs only a narrow procedural task or does not materially influence outcomes (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-6)).

### Core Compliance Obligations
High-risk systems must satisfy risk management (Art. 9), data governance (Art. 10), technical documentation (Art. 11), record-keeping (Art. 12), transparency to deployers (Art. 13), human oversight (Art. 14), and accuracy requirements (Art. 15) (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act-explorer)). Providers face separate obligations under Article 16, including quality management systems (Art. 17), documentation retention (Art. 18), and automated logging (Art. 19) (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-16)). Deployers carry obligations under Article 26, including corrective actions, duty of information (Art. 20), and cooperation with authorities (Art. 21) (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/recital-96)). Article 27 obliges certain deployers to conduct a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment before initial deployment (high confidence) ([EDPB](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/system/files/2025-06/spe-training-on-ai-and-data-protection-legal_en.pdf)). Organizations must also ensure AI literacy among relevant staff under Article 4 (medium confidence) ([Futurium](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/el/apply-ai-alliance/community-content/eu-ai-act-and-recruitment-why-december-2027-extension-prep-window-not-free-pass)). GDPR Article 22 restrictions on fully automated decisions continue to apply alongside these obligations (low confidence) ([Truffle](https://www.hiretruffle.com/blog/eu-ai-act-hiring)).

### Timeline and Enforcement Dates
This is the most contested area. The Digital Omnibus on AI has reportedly deferred Annex III high-risk obligations, including hiring tools, from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027 (high confidence) ([Futurium](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/el/apply-ai-alliance/community-content/eu-ai-act-and-recruitment-why-december-2027-extension-prep-window-not-free-pass), [EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52025PC0836)). The AI Act Service Desk timeline corroborates this, while noting Annex I product-embedded systems take effect 2 August 2028 (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/faq/when-does-ai-act-go-effect-what-its-timeline-implementation)). Conversely, several commercial/legal sources maintain that operational enforcement begins 2 August 2026, with market surveillance authorities gaining full investigatory powers then (medium confidence) ([Heymilo](https://blog.heymilo.ai/how-the-eu-ai-act-changes-recruitment-and-what-employers-need-to-know)). Separately, Article 50 transparency notices to candidates are described as effective August 2026 (medium confidence), and Article 50(2) marking obligations have a 2 December 2026 deadline for systems placed on market before 2 August 2026 (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/faq)).

### Penalties
Non-compliance with high-risk obligations can draw fines up to €15 million or 3% of global turnover (low confidence, due to source weakness) ([Heymilo](https://blog.heymilo.ai/how-the-eu-ai-act-changes-recruitment-and-what-employers-need-to-know)). Prohibited practices (e.g., workplace emotion recognition) can draw fines up to €35 million or 7% of turnover (medium confidence) ([Governance Docs](https://governancedocs.com/eu-ai-act-penalties)). Misleading information to authorities can draw fines up to €7.5 million or 1% of turnover (low confidence) ([Compyl](https://compyl.com/blog/eu-ai-act-penalties)).

### Institutional Enforcement
National market surveillance authorities, not the European Commission directly, will conduct most investigations under Regulation 2019/1020 (low confidence, dated source) ([Orrick](https://www.orrick.com/en/Insights/2024/09/The-EU-AI-Act-Oversight-and-Enforcement)). Germany's Cabinet adopted a draft AI Market Surveillance Act in February 2026 designating the Bundesnetzagentur, but it has not yet passed parliament (medium confidence) ([AI Act Explorer](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/national-implementation-plans)).

### Enforcement Actions to Date
No source documents any actual fine or sanction against a company for AI hiring tool non-compliance (high confidence), across all reviewed sources including EU guidance and legal analyses ([Futurium](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/el/apply-ai-alliance/community-content/eu-ai-act-and-recruitment-why-december-2027-extension-prep-window-not-free-pass), [Heymilo](https://blog.heymilo.ai/how-the-eu-ai-act-changes-recruitment-and-what-employers-need-to-know), [Governance Docs](https://governancedocs.com/eu-ai-act-penalties)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
- **Enforcement date conflict**: Sources diverge sharply between 2 December 2027 (Digital Omnibus-adjusted) and 2 August 2026 (original Annex III date), with unclear reconciliation of how Article 50 transparency deadlines interact with the deferred timeline.
- **SME/small mid-cap fine rule discrepancy**: Heymilo describes the "whichever is lower" fine calculation exception as applying only to SMEs/startups ([Heymilo](https://blog.heymilo.ai/how-the-eu-ai-act-changes-recruitment-and-what-employers-need-to-know)), while Governance Docs states the Digital Omnibus extended this exception to small mid-cap companies as of July 2026 ([Governance Docs](https://governancedocs.com/eu-ai-act-penalties)). This suggests Heymilo's content predates the Digital Omnibus amendment, but neither source clarifies the precise scope or legal basis of the extension, leaving the applicable fine-calculation rule for mid-sized companies uncertain.
- Low-confidence claims (below 0.4) include: penalty amounts for standard non-compliance (0.17), national enforcement authority structure (0.10), fine-rule extension to small mid-caps (0.12), GDPR Article 22 interplay (0.12), and the 2025 penalty start-date claim (0.10)—all requiring caution.
- EU Service Desk FAQ pages appear inconsistently updated to reflect the Digital Omnibus change.

## Knowledge Gaps
No confirmed enforcement actions exist against any company; the Digital Omnibus's formal legislative status and scope of deferral remain unclear; FRIA deadline interaction with the deferred timeline is unaddressed; and most Member States' designation of competent authorities (beyond Germany) is undocumented.
